It was President Hồ Chí Minh himself who personally renamed the road Thanh Nien Road, recognizing the enthusiasm and dedication of the young people who built it.
The history of Thanh Nien Road dates back to the Ly Dynasty when it was originally known as Co Ngut Slope. This ancient slope had a legend associated with a dog that founded the Thang Long Citadel.

The origins of Thanh Nien Road date back to the early 17th century when it was initially constructed as a dam to retain fish in Ho Truc Bach lake. Originally named "Co Ngut," meaning "to keep firm," the name was later mispronounced as "Co Ngu."

In the 17th century, local fishermen built a small embankment from Yen Hoa (Yen Phu) to Yen Ninh to avoid going around, which eventually became the embankment known as Co Ngut, meaning to keep it stable. At this corner of the lake, there was once a palace for Lord Trinh Doanh, which later became a place to house concubines who were either guilty or elderly.

Over time, this road evolved into a vital pathway connecting the two lakes. In the mid-17th century, during the reign of King Le Than Tong, a dike was built from Yen Hoa to Yen Ninh to improve accessibility, and this dike was later fortified and expanded to form part of the outer wall of the Thang Long Citadel under the Le Dynasty.

During the French colonial period, the name "Cau Ngu" emerged due to linguistic differences, and it gradually became the commonly used term for the road.

In 1958, shortly after the liberation of Hanoi, the municipal government initiated a project to widen and improve the road, which was completed by the youth of Hanoi in 1959. To honor their efforts, Ho Chi Minh, the revered leader of Vietnam, renamed the road "Thanh Nien," meaning Youth Road.

To the east of Thanh Nien Road, the Thuy Trung Tien Shrine adds another layer of historical significance. Established more than 900 years ago, this shrine has witnessed the changing fortunes of Hanoi through the ages.
